The study used three materials: aluminum, carbon-fiber reinforced composites, and a hypothetical carbon nanotube composite.
The wing geometry used is the Quasi-CRM (QCRM) with a 30 m semi-span and 35° quarter-chord sweep.
Aerodynamic analysis employed both a medium-fidelity panel method (TriPan) and a high-fidelity CFD solver (SUmb).
Structural analysis was performed with TACS using a smeared stiffness approach for stiffened thin-walled composite structures.
Design variables included aerodynamic shape, structural sizing, and ply angle fractions for composites.
Optimization objectives were to minimize structural weight and fuel burn under stress and buckling constraints.
Composite wings showed consistently lower fuel burn and structural weight than metallic wings.
The carbon nanotube composite did not provide the expected performance gains over carbon-fiber composites.
Aerostructural coupling was fully captured using static aeroelastic analysis to account for wing flexibility.
Adjoint-based gradient methods were used for efficient sensitivity analysis in the high-dimensional design space.
The QCRM wing is untwisted and uses NASA super-critical airfoil sections SC(2)-0414 and SC(2)-0610.
The structural model includes two spars, 44 ribs, and top and bottom wing skins, with non-structural elements for load transfer.
The structural finite-element model had roughly 218,500 degrees of freedom in the smaller model and 453,000 in the refined model.
Drag build-up in the aerodynamic model includes induced drag, skin friction, profile drag, and compressibility drag corrections.
The load transfer scheme uses rigid links to extrapolate structural displacements to aerodynamic nodes.
Newton-Krylov methods with Krylov subspace solvers (GMRES) were used for solving aerodynamic and structural linear systems.
The study generated Pareto fronts to analyze trade-offs between structural weight and fuel burn.
Manufacturing constraints limited thickness changes between adjacent structural components.
The study was funded by NASA under grant NNX11AI19A and conducted at the University of Michigan.
The study highlights the challenge of designing optimal flexible wings in the transonic regime requiring high-fidelity models.
